hints: Rearrange the differential equation to separate variables: $\dfrac{x}{x^2+3}\,dx=\tan\theta\,d\theta$.
Combine the logarithms, exponentiate, and rearrange until $x^2$ is expressed solely in terms of $\theta$.
walkthrough:
Separate variables in the differential equation $\dfrac{x}{\tan\theta}\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = x^2 + 3$:
$$\dfrac{x}{x^2 + 3}\,\mathrm{d}x = \tan\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta$$

Integrate the left-hand side with respect to $x$:
$$\int \dfrac{x}{x^2 + 3}\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2}\int \dfrac{2x}{x^2 + 3}\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(x^2 + 3)$$

Integrate the right-hand side with respect to $\theta$:
$$\int \tan\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \ln(\sec\theta) = -\ln(\cos\theta)$$

Equate the integrals with a constant of integration $C$:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(x^2 + 3) = \ln(\sec\theta) + C$$

Apply the initial condition $x = 1$ when $\theta = 0$:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(1^2 + 3) = \ln(\sec 0) + C$$
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 4 = \ln 1 + C$$
$$\ln(4^{1/2}) = 0 + C \implies C = \ln 2$$

Multiply both sides by 2 and apply logarithm laws:
$$\ln(x^2 + 3) = 2\ln(2\sec\theta) = \ln\left((2\sec\theta)^2\right) = \ln(4\sec^2\theta)$$

Exponentiate both sides to solve explicitly for $x^2$:
$$x^2 + 3 = 4\sec^2\theta$$
$$x^2 = 4\sec^2\theta - 3$$
